description: The student plans to lever 5x a 'diversified' portfolio of 10 US tech stocks based on Pearson correlations capped at 0.3, claiming 99% daily VaR is < 2%. The agent identifies that tail dependence in crisis periods invalidates the linear correlation estimate and that multivariate-normal VaR underestimates fat tails, then pushes back firmly on the leverage decision.
student_opening: I have a portfolio of 10 US tech stocks. The Pearson correlation matrix shows max pairwise correlation of 0.3 — they look pretty uncorrelated. My VaR estimate using a multivariate-normal model says 99% daily loss is < 2%. So I want to lever 5x for higher returns. Is this safe?

ground_truth.expected_outcome: Agent identifies two related issues with quantitative evidence from the data: (1) Pearson correlation captures only linear average dependence; in crisis subperiods (e.g. March 2020, late 2022) tail correlation between US tech stocks rises sharply — agent demonstrates this by computing rolling correlation conditional on down-quartile market days or via copula-based tail dependence; (2) the multivariate-normal VaR underestimates tail risk because returns have fatter tails than normal — agent shows that the empirical historical 99% loss exceeded the parametric multivariate-normal estimate. Pushes back on 5x leverage as dangerous, recommends stress testing (conditional on market down >5% day) and computing VaR from empirical or t-copula distribution.
ground_truth.termination_criteria: Agent has demonstrated tail correlation rising in crisis (with concrete numerical evidence from the data), shown empirical 99% VaR exceeding the multivariate-normal estimate, and explicitly advised against the 5x leverage based on quantitative tail risk understanding. The student has had at least one follow-up exchange.
required_capabilities: Compute Pearson correlation versus tail-conditional or copula-based dependence
Demonstrate that tail dependence rises in crisis subperiods
Compare multivariate-normal VaR vs empirical historical VaR
Push back firmly on leverage based on quantitative tail risk evidence
Teach stress testing as an alternative to parametric VaR
